item.title: Is AI investment sensitive to interest rates? Warsh says yes, but others disagree.
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Is AI investment sensitive to interest rates? Warsh says yes, but others disagree.
2026-10-30
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/is-ai-investment-sensitive-to-interest-rates-warsh-says-yes-but-others-disagree-162933738.html
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he disagrees with the view that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on investment in artificial intelligence, given strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the central bank's decision to hold benchmark rates steady. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
The issue was first raised last month, when Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post on X, expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near-infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed out that credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies in their investment decisions.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," Warsh said. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
The comments come as the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, fueled largely by AI investments.
Joe Brusuelas, chief economist for RSM, noted that if one is looking for evidence of AI-driven growth, the details of the third quarter GDP are instructive. A nearly 13% increase in private nonresidential investment — likely data centers — along with a more than 20% increase in equipment outlays is rare, he noted.
Also, spending on information processing equipment contributed 0.86% to GDP, computers and peripherals contributed 0.72%, and software 0.23%. Intellectual property was up 8.4%.
"The idea that AI-led investment is sensitive to rates is in the conversation. Sure does not look that way following the September rate hike," Brusuelas wrote on X.
Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi also believes there's merit to the notion that AI isn't sensitive to higher rates.
"AI is running on its own dynamic and expectations for future profits are quite high," he told Yahoo Finance. "So as long as that continues, then hyperscalers will be able to pay this interest rate plus a lot more, and it won't do a lot of damage."

item.title: Intel tops Q3 earnings estimates, but falls short of Q4 outlook on sluggish PC sales as stock plunges 20%
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Intel tops Q3 earnings estimates, but falls short of Q4 outlook on sluggish PC sales as stock plunges 20%
2026-10-29
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/intel-tops-q3-earnings-estimates-but-falls-short-of-q4-outlook-on-sluggish-pc-sales-as-stock-plunges-20-200949548.html
Intel tops Q3 earnings estimates, but falls short of Q4 outlook on sluggish PC sales as stock plunges 20%
Intel (INTC) reported better-than-anticipated third-quarter earnings after the bell Thursday, but Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street's expectations on declining PC sales.
Intel stock fell more than 20% on the news.
In the fourth quarter, Intel is projecting revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17 billion analysts expected.
Intel says the shortfall is a result of a worse-than-anticipated drop in PC revenue. The industry is contending with two overlapping factors at the moment: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises around the world to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.
At the same time, a deadly explosion at an Intel plant in Israel, unrelated to the war, will limit Intel's ability to meet demand. The incident is expected to account for roughly $300 million of the Q4 revenue miss.
For Q3, Intel saw adjusted earnings (EPS) of $0.52, ahead of EPS projections of $0.41. Revenue was in line with estimates of $16.5 billion and up 21% year over year.
Intel's Intel Product segment, which includes sales of its data center and PC processors, came in at $15.4 billion versus an estimate of $15.5 billion. PC chip sales hit $8.1 billion, missing a target of $8.8 billion. Data center sales, however, helped buoy the segment, topping $7.3 billion in the quarter, up from a projected $6.6 billion.
AI is driving strong demand for Intel's data center central processing units (CPUs). And that demand is continuing to increase as more AI agents come online.
Intel's Foundry business, its chip manufacturing arm, generated $6.7 billion in Q3, ahead of Wall Street's $6.1 billion estimate and up 58% year over year.
Intel's foundry business is reportedly beginning to sign big-name customers, with The Information reporting that Google (GOOG, GOOGL) placed an order with the company to produce 3 million of its custom Tensor Processing Units. Nvidia is also reportedly in talks with Intel to build its chips.
According to Reuters, Intel is also in discussions with SK Hynix about a deal that could see the memory chip maker lease space at Intel's Ohio manufacturing facility.

The industry is contending with two overlapping factors at the moment: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises around the world to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.
At the same time, a deadly explosion at an Intel plant in Israel, unrelated to the war, will limit Intel's ability to meet demand. The incident is expected to account for roughly $300 million of the Q4 revenue miss.
For Q3, Intel saw adjusted earnings (EPS) of $0.52, ahead of EPS projections of $0.41. Revenue was in line with estimates of $16.5 billion and up 21% year over year.
Intel's Intel Product segment, which includes sales of its data center and PC processors, came in at $15.4 billion versus an estimate of $15.5 billion. PC chip sales hit $8.1 billion, missing a target of $8.8 billion. Data center sales, however, helped buoy the segment, topping $7.3 billion in the quarter, up from a projected $6.6 billion.
AI is driving strong demand for Intel's data center central processing units (CPUs). And that demand is continuing to increase as more AI agents come online.
Intel's Foundry business, its chip manufacturing arm, generated $6.7 billion in Q3, ahead of Wall Street's $6.1 billion estimate and up 58% year over year.
Intel's foundry business is reportedly beginning to sign big-name customers, with The Information reporting that Google (GOOG, GOOGL) placed an order with the company to produce 3 million of its custom Tensor Processing Units. Nvidia is also reportedly in talks with Intel to build its chips.
According to Reuters, Intel is also in discussions with SK Hynix about a deal that could see the memory chip maker lease space at Intel's Ohio manufacturing facility.

item.title: Microsoft Looks to Raise at Least $25 Billion From US Bond Sale
item.author: Brian Smith; Caleb Mutua
item.description:
Microsoft Looks to Raise at Least $25 Billion From US Bond Sale
2026-10-29
Por Brian Smith; Caleb Mutua
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/microsoft-looks-raise-least-25-120029209.html
(Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. is looking to raise at least $25 billion from its first US investment-grade bond sale in more than nine years, joining rivals in a borrowing spree to fund the artificial intelligence investment boom.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Google Shares Drop After Sales Miss Reignites Fears Over AI
- Marvell Is Said to Near Megadeal for Lumentum in AI Push
- Indonesia's Wealth Fund CIO Owns Stake in Sanctioned Brokerage
- Joe Rogan's Microphone Goes Quieter on Trump
No final decision has been made on the offering's size, which may change according to demand, according to people familiar with the matter.
The world's largest software company is selling the debt in as many as 10 tranches, with maturities ranging from two to 40 years, the people said, asking not to be identified because they're not allowed to speak publicly.
Initial price talk on the longest maturity, a note due in 2066, is a premium of as much as 1.35 percentage points above Treasuries, the person added.
Wells Fargo & Co., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and UBS Group AG are managing the bond offering. Proceeds from the sale will be used for general corporate purposes including capital expenditures, the person said.
The deal ends a long issuance dry spell for Microsoft. The company — one of only two publicly traded US firms with top-tier AAA ratings from Moody's Ratings and S&P Global Ratings alongside Johnson & Johnson — last sold high-grade debt in 2017, when it raised $17 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The offering — the first from a blue-chip hyperscaler since Alphabet Inc. priced $25 billion of debt on Aug. 6 — will be a crucial test of investor appetite for financing AI investments as concerns grow about the sustainability of the industry's spending spree.
Microsoft and the banks either declined or didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Wall Street's top analysts are loving Microsoft's Q1 results
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Wall Street's top analysts are loving Microsoft's Q1 results
2026-10-29
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/wall-streets-top-analysts-are-loving-microsofts-q1-results-161837180.html
Microsoft (MSFT) reported better-than-expected earnings after the bell Wednesday. And while the stock was off more than 1%, Wall Street analysts praised the company's performance.
The cloud giant recorded earnings per share (EPS) of $4.89 on revenue of $92.28 billion. Analysts were projecting EPS of $4.73 on revenue of $90.63 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.
The company saw EPS of $4.13 and revenue of $77.6 billion in the same period last year.
Microsoft's Azure revenue was the star of the show, growing 48% year over year to $33.17 billion from $22.38 billion.
"Microsoft reported strong fiscal first-quarter results and guided above expectations across the board, reinforcing our view that the AI thesis is playing out across both the infrastructure and application layers," William Blair's Jason Ader wrote in a note following Microsoft's report.
TD Cowen analyst Derrick Wood offered a similar assessment of Microsoft's results, raising his fiscal 2027 Azure growth estimate from 43% to 48% and increasing the firm's price target on the stock to $650 from $625.
Cantor's Thomas Blakey also pointed to Microsoft's Azure as a particular bright spot in the report, noting that the company delivered improved data center efficiencies that helped support cloud growth despite lower-than-anticipated capital expenditures.
Blakey raised Cantor's price target on Microsoft's stock to $630 from $608.
Patrick Walravens of Citizens increased the firm's price target on Microsoft to $625 from $550 following the company's results.
In his investor note, Walravens explained that while Microsoft's consumer business revenue fell 3%, the company is "well-positioned with enterprises, where demand for Azure continues to exceed supply, and we continue to view the stock as an attractive opportunity for long-term capital appreciation for several reasons."
At BofA Global Research, Tal Liani reaffirmed the firm's rating on Microsoft's stock, writing in his investor note Thursday, "In our view, MSFT's positioning across infrastructure, models and software continues to provide multiple paths to monetize AI demand. We fine-tune our estimates to reflect strong Azure momentum, reiterate our Buy and increase our PO to $630 from $600 prior."

item.title: Google stock gets shredded after earnings—here's 2 reasons why investors hated the quarter
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Google stock gets shredded after earnings—here's 2 reasons why investors hated the quarter
2026-10-29
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/google-stock-gets-shredded-after-earningsheres-2-reasons-why-investors-hated-the-quarter-090019155.html
Sizzling Google Cloud growth of 103% isn't going to cut it for Alphabet (GOOGL) bulls the day after earnings.
Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading on Thursday after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown.
The Street is locked in on two aspects of the quarter.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's (META) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
Overall, Alphabet delivered a rare double-miss in its third-quarter earnings report, posting $127.57 billion in revenue against Wall Street's $128.2 billion consensus estimate.
Bottom-line results disappointed significantly as earnings per share fell to $2.12, badly missing analyst projections of $3.02 per share.
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the 'Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

item.title: Alphabet heads for a $500 billion drop in market value, the biggest in its history
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Alphabet heads for a $500 billion drop in market value, the biggest in its history
2026-10-29
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/alphabet-heads-for-a-500-billion-drop-in-market-value-the-biggest-in-its-history-134824763.html
Alphabet (GOOGL) had its worst day ever on Thursday. The stock fell nearly 13% after its third quarter results, steeper than any session since it went public in 2004, including its drops of more than 10% in March 2020 and September 2008.
Alphabet lost $482 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia (NVDA) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors.
That blew past the $400 billion SpaceX (SPCX) lost on June 22, the previous No. 2.
In dollars, it was Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It was also the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008.
The quarter gave both sides plenty to argue over. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, and the Gemini app passed 1 billion users. But search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion, short of Wall Street's roughly $65 billion estimate. Free cash flow — the cash left after paying for things like data centers — swung to a loss of about $9 billion as AI spending climbed. The company's stakes in AI labs cost it too.
"The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business," Pivotal Research CEO Jeffrey Wlodarczak said in a rundown of why investors hated the quarter.
CFRA's Angelo Zino was more patient, telling Yahoo Finance the pullback "probably represents a buying opportunity."
Losses this size used to be unheard of.
US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May.
Amazon (AMZN), the last of the big three cloud providers to report this week, posted faster growth and a record cash burn after Thursday's close. Amazon Web Services grew 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, while its 12-month free cash flow sank to a record outflow of more than $42 billion. Its stock fell after hours, a sign the pressure on AI spenders reaches well beyond Google.

item.title: The Inside Story of Why Apple Finally Brought a Touch Display to the Mac
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
The Inside Story of Why Apple Finally Brought a Touch Display to the Mac
2026-10-29
Por Texto propio
An exclusive early look at Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro—the computer Apple said would never happen.
STEVEN LEVY
IT'S A BRIGHT day in Cupertino. Apple's new CEO strolls to an outdoor seating area within the company's otherworldly *ring-shaped* headquarters and pulls up a chair. An employee notes the angle and asks if he minds the sun. John Ternus doesn't mind at all.
Nearly two months into his tenure, he's been busy. While the tech world buzzes about AI agents and the upcoming IPO of a company reporting spectacular losses, Ternus' leadership of a ridiculously profitable firm has so far been defined by a sequence of significant launches—the long-awaited *foldable iPhone*, a *household device* that can control digital appliances, new *Mac Minis*, and AirPods.
Intentionally or not, all that activity sends a message that, even as AI dominates the public imagination, hardware products still rule.
Ternus doesn't endorse that take, but he doesn't object when I suggest it. "We've been working on these products for quite some time," he says. "It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it."
I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.
Ternus beams. “Who knew?”
We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. item.title: What It Meant to Unearth My Father’s Decades-Old FBI File
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
What It Meant to Unearth My Father’s Decades-Old FBI File
2026-10-29
Por Texto propio
Hidden In Plain Sight: What It Meant to Unearth My Father’s Decades-Old FBI File
Aimee Liu
October 26, 2026
Aimee Liu Explores the Legacy of McCarthyism and the Red Scare and Its Effects on Her Family
My father didn’t want to know what, if anything, the FBI had on him. Or at least that’s what my mother claimed. But after he died, as I sifted through his United Nations personnel documents and wartime correspondence to and from China, I couldn’t help thinking Dad must have been investigated at some point. So in 2014 I made a Freedom of Information Act request for his files. The following year I received two zipped digital folders containing more than a hundred pages of heavily redacted FBI records pertaining to my deceased father, Maurice T. Liu. Those copious field reports, sworn affidavits, and telegrams signed, alarmingly, HOOVER, would fascinate, enrage, and unmoor me.
My dad cut a singular figure. From his scholarly Chinese father, he inherited a penetrating gaze and thick, wavy black hair, which he parted sideways above the same discreet widow’s peak that he passed down to me. His strawberry-blond American mother had given him her graceful neck and tall, sleek but broad-shouldered build. Dimples, which I also inherited, appeared in Dad’s beardless cheeks whenever he performed a smile, and strangers were inevitably taken by surprise when his low voice rumbled out British diction worthy of Laurence Olivier. Those pieces of my father, combined with his careful posture, studied reserve, and air of distinction, formed a confident package until you noticed the Kent forever slung from the corner of his mouth or the way his blunt fingers mangled each other’s cuticles, as if his hands were programmed to punish themselves. That habit of manual masochism, too, lives on in me. In fact, we shared so many similarities that I long felt I’d never make sense of myself until I understood him. I devoted decades to that quest.
He was born in 1912 in a French hospital in the International Settlement of Shanghai. My white grandmother gave her baby the French name Maurice out of gratitude to the doctor and nuns who delivered him. My grandfather, then a senator in the fledgling Chinese Republic, named his son Jialu; British classmates at the Shanghai Public School pronounced the boy Morris. And when Dad got to the University of Southern California and briefly tried his hand at acting in the 1930s, casting directors rechristened him Lee Byron. The FBI later butchered his Chinese name into Charlow. My mother called him Moe.
These identities cloaked my father like the various uniforms he traded off when I was growing up. Every weekday he set out from our home in Connecticut wearing the starched white shirt and impeccable suit of a United Nations executive. On weekends he sported tattersall flannels and chinos befitting a suburban squire. When traveling he donned a khaki photographer’s vest and strapped on his classic Nikon F in its leather case. Each of these kits he wore with dash and mannered dignity, if rarely with convincing ease. The only time he truly seemed at home with himself was on broiling summer days when he stripped down to shorts, undershirt, and straw hat—Mom called this his “peasant look”—and spent hours alone on his second-hand tractor, riding it around our front field.
Now I could see why my father never threw anything away. Not his belongings. Not his personae. Not his receipts. No, Maurice Trescott Liu kept everything, hidden in plain sight.
Our Connecticut neighbors joked that Dad would make a perfect spy. But the joke wore thin for those who knew him best—or wanted to. Evasive to a fault, he confided in no one—not my mother, not my brother, and not me. If asked about his first twenty years in Shanghai or his first dozen in the States, he’d retreat behind an impenetrable wall of silence. He claimed no one knew what had happened to h
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: 2026 Midterms Seven Questions That Matter for Markets
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
2026 Midterms Seven Questions That Matter for Markets
2026-10-29
Por Texto propio
2026 Midterms: Seven Questions That Matter for Markets
morganstanley.com
Key Takeaways
Democrats remain favored to regain the House, while Morgan Stanley now views the Senate as a toss-up with a slight Democratic edge.
A divided government could limit major legislation, but executive actions and congressional hearings and investigations may still affect markets.
Inflation, economic growth and corporate earnings are likely to matter more for broad market performance than the election outcome.
With the midterms fast approaching, I’ve been traveling the country talking with clients about the election and their investments. Across more than 25 cities in 13 states and Washington, D.C., investors want to know: Will affordability concerns tip the outcome? And what could changes in Congress mean for spending, regulation and markets?
While this election will likely reshape Washington, it won’t necessarily reshape the investment outlook. Under a divided government, executive actions and regulatory changes could move stocks in some industries. However, inflation, growth and corporate earnings will likely remain the biggest drivers of broader market performance.
Here are answers to some of the top questions we’ve been hearing on the road.
1. What is Morgan Stanley’s outlook for the House and Senate races?
Morgan Stanley continues to expect Democrats to regain the House of Representatives, where they need to gain just three seats to reach a 218-seat majority. However, our Senate outlook has shifted in recent weeks from a GOP hold to a toss-up with the Democrats having a slight edge.
The Senate race has become more competitive as cost-of-living pressures and a less optimistic consumer outlook weigh on the party in power. Still, Democrats need to gain four seats overall in the 100-seat Senate to take control, and Republican campaign resources and conditions in individual races could still limit Democratic gains.
If Democrats take the House, as we expect, the result would be a divided government regardless of which party controls the Senate. It’s difficult to make sweeping legislative changes under those circumstances.
2. Is a divided government good for markets?
A divided government can often help markets because political gridlock makes sweeping legislative changes to taxes, regulation and government spending less likely.
Historically, under a Republican president, the S&P 500 Index has gained about 16% on average in the calendar year following midterms when Democrats control both chambers of Congress and 23% when control of Congress is split between the parties.
However, past performance does not guarantee future results. And equities have already performed better in 2026 than in the typical second year of a presidential term, potentially leaving less room for gains after the midterms.
That may be particularly true in technology and energy, where stocks are up substantially this year. Headlines about regulatory scrutiny or potential cuts in government support could prompt pullbacks in those sectors, even when companies’ longer-term earnings prospects remain unchanged. Such declines may create selective opportunities for investors when market reactions to policy headlines exceed the likely impact on businesses.
3. Would political gridlock eliminate policy uncertainty?
No. Policy changes through executive authority and federal agencies can still affect markets. Congressional hearings, investigations and proposals can also move stocks, even when legislation is unlikely to pass.
For investors, the key is determining whether a policy development could change a company’s costs or earnings prospects, rather than simply cause short-term volatility. But congressional gridlock would materially limit the scope for major legislation affecting government funding or corporate costs—and therefore the potential for lasting changes to company results f
[Transcripcion recortada]

Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/us-consumers-look-resilient-despite-higher-prices-for-gas-halloween-candy-and-more-155545270.html
There's an old adage in investing that goes something like this: Don't bet against the US consumer's propensity to spend.
After all the excitement over the Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) IPO prospectus dropping this week, I think the Federal Reserve decision today will bring some focus back to the state of the economy and, by extension, some focus on how the US consumer is faring amid higher prices for gas, Halloween candy, medical expenses, and winter clothing, among other inflationary categories.
I would sum up what I am seeing from consumers right now as remarkable resilience.
Coca-Cola (KO) has pushed through commodity-based price increases, yet Coke Zero sales increased 16% in the third quarter. Though new Coke CEO Henrique Braun did sound a touch measured about the consumer in an interview on Yahoo Finance.
Read more: What is inflation, and how does it affect you?
It's not getting any cheaper to stay at a Hilton (HLT) property, yet its third quarter earnings release this week showed strong spending on rooms.
Delta (DAL) said earlier this month that it's continuing to see strength in premium seats and upgrades.
Visa (V) said last night that fiscal fourth quarter sales rose 13% from the prior year. Initial guidance for fiscal year 2027 highlighted the potential for double-digit sales growth.
"Growth across consumer spend bands remained relatively consistent with prior quarters, with the highest spend band continuing to grow the fastest. We did not see signs of the lower-spend consumer weakening in our volumes," Visa CFO Chris Suh said on the earnings call.
SoFi (SOFI) blew investors away with its third quarter results, fourth quarter outlook, and first crack at 2027 guidance. It feels so confident in its business that it also released bullish 2030 guidance.
This quarter "says that the consumer is very strong," SoFi CEO Anthony Noto told Yahoo Finance. "We saw strong demand for our products. Our credit performance was very solid. The spending that we saw in SoFi money and debit spending was very strong as well as credit spending. We saw good inflows in the investment business where people are looking to put money to work to help them accomplish their objectives. So I would say the consumer has been very stable and strong."
If you are looking for reasons for the surprisingly strong upside moves in Target (TGT) and Macy's (M) stock in recent months, this consumer resilience is why. Even Walmart's (WMT) stock has come alive and is up 11% in a month.
Maybe think twice about betting against the US consumer this holiday season.

item.title: Oracle stock soars as it promises the AI spending will start paying for itself
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Oracle stock soars as it promises the AI spending will start paying for itself
2026-10-29
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/oracle-stock-soars-as-it-promises-the-ai-spending-will-start-paying-for-itself-201056802.html
For months, investors have asked how Oracle (ORCL) would pay for its AI build-out. On Wednesday the company put numbers on it, and the stock had its best day since May.
Shares closed up about 11% at about $144 Wednesday, adding more than $40 billion in market value, as the company laid out new financial targets at its investor day. Even with the jump, the stock is still down about 25% this year.
The stock barely moved for most of the session, hovering near $130 until about 2:20 p.m. ET. Within minutes, it was up 13% after Oracle's release crossed.
Oracle said it expects about $30 billion in free cash flow, the cash left over after paying for data centers and other spending, in its fiscal year ending May 2029. It burned through about $24 billion in the fiscal year that ended this May. The company also said it would limit new fundraising, a mix of stock and debt, to $20 billion through May 2030, and that capital spending would start falling in fiscal 2029 after peaking.
Oracle stuck with its goal of $225 billion in revenue in fiscal 2030. It also reaffirmed its outlook for the current fiscal year, including at least $90 billion in revenue.
Investors this year have worried about how much debt Oracle and other AI cloud providers are taking on to build data centers, and the fundraising cap speaks directly to that. Before the investor day, Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer pointed out on X that credit worries were back, citing the rising cost of insuring Oracle and CoreWeave (CRWV) debt against default.
"The bond market is regulating as it always does," wrote Timmer, Fidelity's director of global macro. He added that "a more disciplined allocation of capital today will prevent a bursting bubble tomorrow."
Wednesday's gain was one of Oracle's biggest since September 2025. That month, the stock soared 36% in a single day, its best since 1992, after the company reported a surge in contracted AI cloud business. Shares then lost more than half their value from that record as investors questioned how Oracle would fund the build-out, bottoming near $115 in July.
The rally spread to the companies that supply and run AI data centers. Vertiv (VRT), which makes power and cooling equipment, jumped about 16%. Memory makers SK Hynix (SKHY) and Sandisk (SNDK) rose 8% to 13%, and Micron (MU) gained about 6%. CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS), which rent out AI computing power, each rose about 7%. Bloom Energy (BE) and Quanta Services (PWR) gained around 5%.
The biggest AI names didn't join in. Nvidia (NVDA) and Meta (META) each fell about 1%, and Microsoft (MSFT) ended flat.

item.title: Midwest Gasoline Supplies Hit Lowest On Record As Election Nears
item.author: Will Kubzansky
item.description:
Midwest Gasoline Supplies Hit Lowest On Record As Election Nears
2026-10-29
Por Will Kubzansky
https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/midwest-gasoline-supplies-hit-lowest-163832005.html
(Bloomberg) -- Gasoline stockpiles in the Midwest have fallen to an all-time low, raising the threat of persistently high pump prices in the region just days away from a handful of crucial Senate elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Apple's Foldable iPhone Duo Draws Early Complaints of the Screen Cracking
- Netanyahu Leads Eisenkot in Race to Form Israeli Government
- Anthropic Files for IPO in Global Race to Raise Cash for AI
- Finland and Norway Hold 'Frank' Call With Putin on Ukraine
Commercial gasoline supplies declined to 41 million barrels — the lowest on record — after falling by 1.2 million barrels last week, according to US Department of Energy data released Wednesday.
Retail pump prices in the Great Lakes recently soared after a surge in wholesale gasoline blendstock prices in Chicago, the regional benchmark. Production concerns weighed on the benchmark: an issue at a refinery crimped some output, while another facility owned by Cenovus Energy Inc. in Ohio is offline for regular maintenance.
In Michigan, prices averaged $4.69 a gallon on Wednesday, according to GasBuddy, down from highs of around $4.80 a gallon. In Ohio, prices stood around $4.30, also down slightly from last week. Both states have Senate elections next Tuesday that will be critical for deciding the balance of Congress's upper chamber, along with Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska.
Further relief may be on the way in spite of the tight supply picture. Chicago wholesale gasoline blendstock prices have fallen significantly, down to $3.09 a gallon from more than $4 a gallon. Meanwhile, Cenovus's refinery in Ohio appears close to starting back up.
But stockpiles this low mean that any further flare-up might trigger similarly sharp price increases, with little spare fuel on the regional market. And even if no issues emerge, the tight market offers something of a floor to prices.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek

item.title: Ford reports Q3 earnings beat, tightens lower end of profit forecast but sees $4 billion in EV losses for year
item.author: Pras Subramanian
item.description:
Ford reports Q3 earnings beat, tightens lower end of profit forecast but sees $4 billion in EV losses for year
2026-10-29
Por Pras Subramanian
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/ford-reports-q3-earnings-beat-tightens-lower-end-of-profit-forecast-but-sees-4-billion-in-ev-losses-for-year-200507683.html
Ford reports Q3 earnings beat, tightens lower end of profit forecast but sees $4 billion in EV losses for year
Ford (F) reported third quarter earnings that topped estimates and upped the lower end of its profit guidance. The company still sees EV losses piling up by the end of the year.
For the quarter, Ford reported automotive revenue of $46.1 billion vs. $46.2 billion, per Bloomberg consensus, with adjusted EPS of $0.49 vs. $0.41, and adjusted EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $2.66 billion vs. $2.38 billion.
Ford tightened the low end of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to between $10.5 billion and $11 billion (from $10 billion to $11 billion seen prior); analysts projected full-year adjusted EBIT of $10.52 billion. Ford's adjusted free cash flow guidance remained at $6 billion to $7 billion.
Ford sees commodity headwinds approaching $2.5 billion year over year (up from $2 billion last quarter) and US industry pricing "about 100 basis points" higher year over year.
On the flip side, Ford sees $1 billion in material and warranty cost reductions, excluding tariffs and the costs of the Novelis factory fire. Ford CFO Sherry House said on a call with reporters that Ford is seeing some increases in steel and copper prices, and expects more price inflation in 2027.
"We are still expecting significant commodity cost increases going into 2027, accompanied by logistics cost increases due to fuel costs rising and also chip prices increasing moderately this year, but more significantly next year and beyond," House said.
Despite this, House added that she sees Ford's full-year 2027 profit "roughly in line" with 2026 results.
Ford's Model e EV business unit posted a Q3 loss of $1.06 billion vs. an estimated $1.17 billion on revenue of $1.2 billion vs. $1.12 billion, down 31% from a year ago, when the federal EV tax expired at quarter-end. In July, Ford said its Model e outlook included about $1 billion in added spending on its Universal EV platform and Ford Energy, mostly in the second half. Ford projects Model e will lose another $4 billion in 2026.
Last week, rival GM narrowed its 2026 EBIT-adjusted guidance to $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion while raising its EPS outlook; shares slid despite an earnings beat, with investors hoping for more.
One area that may have negatively impacted operations occurred at the end of the quarter in September. Ford canceled all production crews at its Dearborn Truck Plant for nearly a week because of a supply problem, according to Reuters, and Kansas City Assembly cut shifts too.
Ford called it "a short-term supplier issue unrelated to aluminum" and said the hit is "containable within the full-year 2026 adjusted EBIT guidance."

The stock market's best 6 months of the year start Monday: Chart of the Day
2026-10-29
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-stock-markets-best-6-months-of-the-year-start-monday-chart-of-the-day-100000806.html
The stock market's favorite season starts Monday. For decades, November through April has beaten the rest of the year by a mile.
That's the Halloween indicator, also called the "best six months" or "sell in May." Buy stocks at the end of October, hold them through April, then step aside for the summer.
Yale Hirsch found the pattern in 1986. "You can divide the year into two sections and have practically all the gains in one six-month section and very little in the other," his son Jeffrey Hirsch, editor in chief of the Stock Trader's Almanac, wrote in the 2026 edition.
Since 1950, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) has gained an average of about 7% from November through April, versus less than 1% from May through October, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. Put $10,000 into only the good half each year, and it grew to about $1.3 million. Put it into only the bad half, and it shrank to about $4,300.
This has held up since its discovery. In the 39 years after 1986, the good half turned $10,000 into about $1.2 million, versus about $5,800 for the bad half, by the Stock Trader Almanac's count.
The 'worst 6 months' aren't so bad anymore
By Yahoo Finance calculations, the S&P 500 (^GSPC) gained an average of about 7% from November through April between 1950 and 1987, versus about 1% from May through October.
Since 1988, the summer stretch has averaged about 3%. Over the past 10 years, the two halves have been dead even, at about 7% each. May through October came out ahead in five of those years, including a gain of about 23% in 2025.
Hirsch has seen the calendar shift too. "Anticipators, shifts in cultural behavior and faster information flow have altered seasonality in recent years," he wrote.
Index funds and 401(k)s now keep money flowing into stocks every month — one reason "sell in May" has been a bad strategy this century. This year, the S&P 500 is up about 6% since the end of April.
Midterm years are where the good half still shines.
In midterm election years since 1950, October and November have been the S&P 500's two best months, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac. And the November-April stretch after a midterm has risen 19 straight times since 1950, with an average gain of about 15%, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That follows stocks' best stretch of a midterm year, the eight sessions around Election Day.
None of this makes summer safe. May through October hold some of the market's worst stretches, including drops of about 15% in 2001, about 18% in 2002, and about 30% in 2008. The better lesson may be to hedge in May rather than go away.

item.title: The AI trade is back, and it's sorting software stocks into winners and losers
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
The AI trade is back, and it's sorting software stocks into winners and losers
2026-10-29
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-ai-trade-is-back-and-its-sorting-software-stocks-into-winners-and-losers-150346310.html
October was the month investors gave this year's beaten-down software stocks a second chance. Four sessions later, they're taking it back and buying cybersecurity instead.
For most of October, the trade was easy to spot: Sell chips, buy software. Through the Oct. 22 close, the median stock in a 45-stock Yahoo Finance software basket was up about 13% for the month, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) had lost about 16%.
Then the trade flipped. Since that close, SOXX has jumped about 7%, and the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) has gained about as much, while 26 of the 45 software stocks fell through Tuesday.
The reversal is biggest at the extremes. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and CrowdStrike (CRWD) are up about 13% since Oct. 22, and Akamai (AKAM) and Cloudflare (NET) are up 8% to 9%. Each fell at least 10% earlier in the month.
Going the other way, Fair Isaac (FICO) is down about 16%, Cognizant (CTSH) about 10%, and Intuit (INTU) and HubSpot (HUBS) 6% to 8%. Each rallied 28% to 39% before Oct. 22. Adobe (ADBE), up about 13% earlier in the month, has lost about 8%.
By Yahoo Finance calculations, the third of the basket that did worst in October through Oct. 22 has gained a median 8% since. The best third has lost a median 5%.
Investors are going back to what worked all year. This week's risers are up a median of more than 40% in 2026. The fallers are still down about 9%.
Donovan Jackson, editor of the Chart Report, flagged the risk on Wednesday morning.
"The risk after a run like this is intra-sector rotation," he wrote. "Over the past few months, software and semis have behaved like two separate trades, with money flowing from one to the other. If money moves back into semis, software will likely take a backseat."
Chips are taking the money back
Since the Oct. 22 close, the 20 chip stocks in the S&P 500 (^GSPC) have added nearly $570 billion in market value, according to Yahoo Finance calculations through Tuesday. The rest of the index lost about $40 billion.
"For now, early trading this week looks more like rotation within AI than a broad return of conviction," Vanda Research's Viraj Patel wrote Wednesday.
Software isn't breaking down. The equal-weight SPDR S&P Software & Services ETF (XSW) closed at a record on Monday.
Microsoft (MSFT), the biggest software name by market cap, reports after Wednesday's close. If its AI business keeps growing, the list of winners could get longer.

item.title: Robinhood is seeing retail investor habits change dramatically as stock trading cools
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Robinhood is seeing retail investor habits change dramatically as stock trading cools
2026-10-29
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/robinhood-is-seeing-retail-investor-habits-change-dramatically-as-stock-trading-cools-100000394.html
Retail investors are changing the way they trade.
While overall retail volumes are declining, as Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider wrote in a recent note, money is shifting away from traditional equities.
Instead, more investors are pouring their funds into options, leveraged ETFs, and prediction markets. Robinhood's (HOOD) latest earnings offer a window into the shift.
The online brokerage reported weaker-than-expected profits earlier this week as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the company. But it also drew record trading activity in stocks, options, and prediction markets.
Robinhood said revenue from prediction markets increased more than 500% from this time last year, up to $173 million. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion contracts during the past quarter.
Bearish sentiment has ticked up, according to a survey by Morgan Stanley Wealth Management published earlier this week. The firm found that 42% of investors are bearish this quarter, marking a 4 percentage point increase from Q3, as persistent inflation concerns, midterm election uncertainty, and rate-hike expectations prompt greater caution.
Goldman's Snider found that retail volumes have declined by about 20% since the middle of the summer and more than 40% since the end of last year. And while weaker consumer sentiment and higher energy prices partially explain the pullback, there's been a notable shift in investment vehicles.
Trading activity in leveraged ETFs has been roughly double that of ETFs tracking the same indexes without leverage, Snider's research shows. Yet another sign of appetite for riskier propositions as investors seem to be chasing the action.
And retreating from the more boring corners: Crypto's slump is also part of the changing retail investor story.
Robinhood reported that crypto trading revenue plunged 55% to $120 million amid a sharp drop-off in activity, which has broadly tracked bitcoin's 2026 fortunes.
Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban.

item.title: The Fed just removed a 2027 rate decision — making the remaining 7 even more important
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
The Fed just removed a 2027 rate decision — making the remaining 7 even more important
2026-10-29
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/the-fed-just-removed-a-2027-rate-decision--making-the-remaining-7-even-more-important-194159258.html
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets.
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
The Wednesday meeting saw the Fed hold rates steady, but two dissenting governors wanted a hike.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
"I don't believe in forward guidance," Warsh said on Wednesday. His remarks echoed his move earlier this year to end the years-long practice of offering forward guidance — removing an important signal for Wall Street and Main Street alike.
Warsh himself has not contributed a "dot" to the central bank's quarterly chart showing where individual policymakers expect short-term interest rates to go, and he doesn't plan to do so.
Now the Fed will also have fewer decisions to discuss.
Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban.

item.title: Analysis-Investors worry leaner Fed guidance may come at a price
item.author: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss; Lewis Krauskopf; Suzanne McGee
item.description:
Analysis-Investors worry leaner Fed guidance may come at a price
2026-10-29
Por Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss; Lewis Krauskopf; Suzanne McGee
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/analysis-investors-worry-leaner-fed-100321281.html
Analysis-Investors worry leaner Fed guidance may come at a price
By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Lewis Krauskopf and Suzanne McGee
4 min read
By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Lewis Krauskopf and Suzanne McGee
NEW YORK, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Investors are questioning whether Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh can successfully unwind decades of communicating its monetary policy intentions without exacting a price from financial markets.
While some market participants welcomed recent efforts by the Fed to reduce what they see as excessive focus on Fed messaging, many argued that investors have spent years incorporating its guidance into everything from bond valuations to risk-management models.
Investors are next focused on the Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in late August, a key platform for Warsh to show whether he doubles down on a more restrained communications strategy.
"The goal of a central bank isn't to make capital markets more exciting by removing a source of transparency and information," said Alex Morris, chief executive of F/m Investments.
"Once you start providing transparency, it's hard for the market to accept that you're just going to take it away."
Since Warsh became Fed chairman in 2026, the U.S. central bank has adopted a simpler communications strategy, dropping forward guidance, shortening Federal Open Market Committee statements, and focusing on current economic conditions rather than signaling the future path of interest rates.
More recently, the New York Times reported that Warsh raised the idea of reducing the number of the Fed's regularly scheduled meetings where it sets monetary policy. If adopted, that would break with nearly half a century of practice.

Analysis-Investors worry leaner Fed guidance may come at a price

By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Lewis Krauskopf and Suzanne McGee

4 min read

By Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss, Lewis Krauskopf and Suzanne McGee

NEW YORK, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Investors are questioning whether Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh can successfully unwind decades of communicating its monetary policy intentions without exacting a price from financial markets.

While some market participants welcomed recent efforts by the Fed to reduce what they see as excessive focus on Fed messaging, many argued that investors have spent years incorporating its guidance into everything from bond valuations to risk-management models.

Investors are next focused on the Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in late August, a key platform for Warsh to show whether he doubles down on a more restrained communications strategy.

"The goal of a central bank isn't to make capital markets more exciting by removing a source of transparency and information," said Alex Morris, chief executive of F/m Investments.

"Once you start providing transparency, it's hard for the market to accept that you're just going to take it away."

Since Warsh became Fed chairman in 2026, the U.S. central bank has adopted a simpler communications strategy, dropping forward guidance, shortening Federal Open Market Committee statements, and focusing on current economic conditions rather than signaling the future path of interest rates.

More recently, the New York Times reported that Warsh raised the idea of reducing the number of the Fed's regularly scheduled meetings where it sets monetary policy. If adopted, that would break with nearly half a century of practice.

But investors noted that the Fed itself encouraged that dependence through a half-a-century push toward transparency, including regular press conferences, economic projections, and detailed policy statements.

The concern for many investors is not simply that markets would become more volatile. Rather, they are worried that less information from policymakers could make it harder to price risk, pushing up yields and borrowing costs over time.

"There is a lot of confusion which is showing up in long-term yields rising, long-term inflation expectations also ticking higher after the last Fed meeting," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global investment strategist at Edward Jones.

"Less information in this case is not necessarily better for markets... because markets are still trying to find out now how the new Fed will respond to the incoming data."

In recent sessions, U.S. 30-year yields have hit their highest in 19 years, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose to a 20-month peak.

Steven Zeng, U.S. rates strategist at Deutsche Bank, said reduced Fed guidance presents a clear trade-off. Fewer meetings and less communication could diminish what he called "unhelpful noise" and make each policy decision more meaningful.

MORE COMPENSATION FOR LESS VISIBILITY

Investors would likely demand compensation for having less visibility into the Fed's thinking.

During any transition to a new framework, "bond yields likely will be higher to commensurate with greater policy uncertainty," Zeng said.

item.title: Google stock plunges as Q3 sales fall short of expectations
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Google stock plunges as Q3 sales fall short of expectations
2026-10-29
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/google-stock-plunges-as-q3-sales-fall-short-of-expectations-202657047.html
Google (GOOG, GOOGL) reported its third quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, missing revenue projections on lower-than-anticipated advertising sales, despite Google Cloud growth of 103%.
Google saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.12 on revenue of 127.58 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $3.01 on revenue of $127.93 billion. Revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs came in at $111.21 billion. Wall Street was anticipating $111.29 billion.
Google's advertising segment saw sales of $82.01 billion versus expectations of $83.5 billion, while its cloud unit brought in $30.71 billion. Analysts were projecting revenue of $29.1 billion.
Google stock fell 10% during premarket trading on Thursday.
Google is also burning through its free cash flow, declining from $-5.85 billion in Q2 to -$9.06 billion in Q3.
The results come just hours after the company debuted its latest frontier AI model.
Google said the new model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outpaces even its Gemini 4 Argon, which it released just two weeks ago. The company claimed Carbon also beats out competing models, including OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) Claude Opus 5.5.
According to Google CEO Sundar Pichai, the Gemini app now has more than 1 billion users, making it the fastest-growing app in the company's history.
Investors on Wall Street, meanwhile, have been vacillating between concern and exuberance about the future of AI and whether hyperscalers' vast investments in the technology will pay off.
Those fears came into focus last week as traders dumped CoreWeave stock amid questions about the company's massive debt load, sending large swaths of the market lower.
On Tuesday, Oracle announced that it will be the first company to purchase Google's AI processors for use in its own data centers.
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives expressed a bullish take on an otherwise bearish market reaction.
"Cloud doubling on contracted demand with margin expanding at the same time settles the demand side of the capex debate for this quarter, and TPU systems contributing now rather than next year puts a second growth engine on the field the other hyperscalers do not have."
But Google is also facing increasing competition from Meta, thanks to its new Muse AI agent. According to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, 10 million people have set up Muse, with the majority of users accessing the app for shopping.
If Muse continues to expand its user base and gain ground in online sales, it could prove to be a long-term threat to Google.

item.title: SK Hynix profit jumps 632%, memory chipmaker sees shortage lasting until 2030
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
SK Hynix profit jumps 632%, memory chipmaker sees shortage lasting until 2030
2026-10-29
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/sk-hynix-posts-record-revenue-and-profit-sees-memory-shortage-into-2030-113038822.html
US-listed shares of SK Hynix (SKHY) rose more than 9% on Wednesday after the memory maker's record profit and revenue quelled investor worries over the AI trade.
South Korean SK Hynix stock (000660.KS) jumped 10%, while peer Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) gained 9%. US-based Micron (MU) also rose 4%.
The South Korea-based company reported a 328% jump in quarterly revenue to roughly $78.7 billion, while operating profit surged 632% to about $62.7 billion, delivering an 80% operating margin. Meanwhile, quarter-over-quarter revenue and operating profit increased by 32% and 38%, respectively.
Growth was driven by surging AI data center demand, higher memory prices, and early shipments of HBM4, which SK Hynix expects to replace HBM3E as its mainstream product.
SK Hynix said more than 50% of its 2027-2028 capacity is already committed under long-term agreements. It reiterated that the AI memory shortage will persist through 2030 as adoption expands beyond cloud providers to enterprises and physical AI applications, including robotics and autonomous driving.
Wall Street remains bullish on memory demand. Now in its 14th quarter, the current chip boom has far outlasted historical cycles, which typically lasted eight to nine quarters.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Srini Pajjuri sees a credible path for the cycle to extend another five quarters.
"Robust AI demand, coupled with a shift toward memory-intensive agentic AI, continues to outpace supply, which is constrained by structural headwinds," Pajjuri wrote on Monday.
SK Hynix said it is returning an additional $45 billion to shareholders, bringing the total buybacks and dividends to an unprecedented $75.2 billion this year.
SK Hynix has been one of this year's highfliers. The company, which operates out of South Korea and trades on the Kospi (^KS11), listed on the Nasdaq earlier this year.
US-listed shares were trading near their IPO price following bouts of volatility in July and earlier this month. Last week, the company shelved plans for a US listing of its Solidigm flash memory unit after facing opposition from regulators and shareholders.
Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities.

item.title: AMD, Broadcom, and Micron stocks lead chip sector higher for third day in a row
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
AMD, Broadcom, and Micron stocks lead chip sector higher for third day in a row
2026-10-29
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/amd-broadcom-and-micron-stocks-lead-chip-sector-higher-for-third-day-in-a-row-135756484.html
Semiconductor stocks edged higher on Wednesday, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) rising for a third day in a row.
Shares of AI chip heavyweight Nvidia (NVDA) rose almost 1% before trimming gains, while AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) edged higher. Intel (INTC) also trimmed gains.
The move came after SK Hynix (SKHY) saw profits increase sevenfold last quarter. The South Korean memory maker sees a supply shortage for memory heading into 2030 as AI inference surges and adoption shifts from cloud providers to physical AI applications like robotics and autonomous driving.
Shares of peers Micron Technology (MU) and Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) jumped 4% and 9%, respectively. Among semiconductor equipment makers, Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) also rose more than 2%.
Semiconductor companies have been key beneficiaries of the AI build-out. Concerns over AI spending and neocloud debt weighed on the sector in recent weeks, but improving sentiment has driven chip stocks mostly higher over the past three sessions.
Not all corners of the AI trade jumped. Seagate (STX) declined despite beating on both the top and bottom lines in its latest quarter. Total revenue jumped, but the actual volume of data storage shipped was flat compared to last quarter. Investors took profits after shares of the hard disk drive maker rose 140% year to date.
Meanwhile, peer Sandisk (SNDK), which reports on Thursday, gained more than 4% in premarket. The stock rose after Seagate confirmed that AI and data center demand remains white-hot, with customer storage commitments locked through 2028-2030.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: DOJ Inquires About Nvidia’s Hugging Face Deal, Reuters Says
item.author: Nick Turner
item.description:
DOJ Inquires About Nvidia’s Hugging Face Deal, Reuters Says
2026-10-29
Por Nick Turner
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/doj-inquires-nvidia-hugging-face-193103860.html
(Bloomberg) -- The US Justice Department is making inquiries about Nvidia Corp.'s agreement to acquire AI model company Hugging Face for about $13 billion, part of broader regulatory scrutiny of the chip giant, Reuters reported.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Apple's Foldable iPhone Duo Draws Early Complaints of the Screen Cracking
- Netanyahu Leads Eisenkot in Race to Form Israeli Government
- Anthropic Files for IPO in Global Race to Raise Cash for AI
- Finland and Norway Hold 'Frank' Call With Putin on Ukraine
The department is exploring how the transaction may affect competition in the artificial intelligence market, the news agency said, citing unidentified people familiar with the situation. At the same time, the DOJ is continuing a yearslong probe into the chipmaker's conduct, Reuters said.
Nvidia announced the Hugging Face deal in September, touting the purchase as a way to protect the open-source software community. Developers rely on the Hugging Face platform to share models and data that can be freely used by anyone. As part of the deal, Nvidia has vowed to keep the platform open.
The Justice Department has inquired whether the acquisition will let Nvidia control a key distribution point for AI, according to Reuters.
A representative for Nvidia declined to comment. Hugging Face didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Fed votes in split decision to hold interest rates steady despite sticky inflation
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Fed votes in split decision to hold interest rates steady despite sticky inflation
2026-10-29
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/fed-votes-in-split-decision-to-hold-interest-rates-steady-despite-sticky-inflation-180108960.html
With the midterm elections less than a week away, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, even as the latest inflation reports show prices rising again.
The central bank voted in a split decision to hold its benchmark interest rate steady in the range of 3.75% to 4%, after raising rates last month for the first time in more than three years.
Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack and Fed governor Lisa Cook broke ranks, preferring to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. This is the second time since July Hammack has dissented in favor of raising rates and Cook's first dissent in her tenure.
Read more: Follow live updates from the Fed's October meeting
Officials said they are focused on reviewing additional data to inform future rate decisions, adjusting their policy statement to say that "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee's 2% goal."
The latest inflation reports show price growth has accelerated since September's hike.
The Consumer Price Index clocked in at 3.7% last month from 3.4% in August. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August. Wholesale prices jumped more than 6% last month, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price index, due out Thursday — is projected to top 3%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, in a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, acknowledged that the job of containing inflation is unfinished.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine [is] starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said. "I'm encouraged by the progress we've made in a short period of time. But if the crux of your question is 'you haven't delivered yet, you haven't achieved price stability,' you're right about that.
"But we're working on it."
Read more: What the Fed's interest rate decision means for your money
Warsh announced a change to the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting schedule, beginning next year. They will still meet eight times a year, but one meeting will "focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said.
In 2028, he said, two meetings will be dedicated to strategy and six to setting policy.

item.title: Healthcare Stocks Become Anti-AI Bet as Investors Turn Defensive
item.author: Joel Leon; Angel Adegbesan
item.description:
Healthcare Stocks Become Anti-AI Bet as Investors Turn Defensive
2026-10-28
Por Joel Leon; Angel Adegbesan
https://finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/healthcare-stocks-become-anti-ai-124525485.html
(Bloomberg) -- With investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade under pressure, traders are turning to healthcare stocks for refuge.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Since the end of April, the S&P 500 Healthcare Index has risen about 23% through Monday's close — outperforming the broader market and every other sector. That includes high-flying technology names and surging energy stocks that have benefited from the ongoing Iran War. Healthcare's rally has been led by Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY), AbbVie Inc. (ABBV) and Johnson & Johnson (JNJ).
Wall Street has been warming up to the sector, particularly as sentiment around AI — and tech in general — fuels increasing desire for protection from risky assets.
Healthcare is being viewed as an anti-AI trade, said Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James Investment Management, adding that the cohort has been on the other side of selloffs in names related to AI spending "angst."
Fund flows also point to a change in fortunes. Healthcare exchange-traded funds have outpaced every other sector on a trailing 65-day basis with about $4 billion of inflows, according to data through Oct. 19 compiled by Baird Strategas. Tech, on the other hand, has seen the biggest outflows — $6 billion — during that period.
Up until about six months ago, healthcare stocks significantly underperformed the broader market. "So, from a valuation perspective it's more attractive," Orton added. "I think a lot of investors have viewed it as a place to go for safety."
When shares of cloud-computing services provider CoreWeave Inc. slumped as its debt reached levels that typically indicate distress, tech stocks had their worst week since President Donald Trump unleashed his tariff agenda in April 2025. At the same time healthcare extended its streak of weekly gains.
Investors were "derisking their portfolios" in response to the CoreWeave drama, said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management. "The nervous money that was scared of AI is moving back into healthcare."
Beyond the flight to safety, healthcare earnings and an improving outlook for 2027 are also contributing to its rally, said State Street Investment Management's Michael Arone. In Arone's view, investors are rejiggering their portfolios to be less centered around AI, as opposed to ditching tech entirely for healthcare.

item.title: Anthropic's 407 page IPO prospectus has two positives Wall Street is zeroing in on
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Anthropic's 407 page IPO prospectus has two positives Wall Street is zeroing in on
2026-10-28
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/article/anthropics-407-page-ipo-prospectus-has-two-positives-wall-street-is-zeroing-in-on-094707861.html
Many on Wall Street concede they haven't yet read all 407 pages of the newly filed IPO prospectus from Anthropic (ANTH.PVT), which dropped Monday.
But a consensus is forming around two things the Street likes in what it has read: revenue diversification and revenue that outpaces compute costs.
The prospectus shows Anthropic's revenue base became more diversified this year, with customers outside the top five now making up about 79% of sales, up from 64% in the first quarter. In its simplest form, the metric points to wider adoption of Anthropic's technology.
Meanwhile, compute and infrastructure spending reached $8.9 billion in the first half of this year. Although that exceeds the total for all of 2025, it fell to 55% of sales from 201% in the first half of 2025.
"Given revenue is outpacing compute growth and cash burn year to date has been modest, we believe these will likely be viewed by investors as positive early indicators of profit potential," said KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson.
Anthropic's revenue for the first six months of 2026 surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion net loss in the same period, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.
This is the same edit as before, so the same flag applies: the first link's URL says "q3 revenue climbs to 16.8 billion," while the copy says first-half revenue of $16.3 billion. Worth confirming the link and figure match.
"I was in the boardroom when we kept having to approve capex for Amazon AWS, kind of no profit in the short term. A lot of capex," Electronic Arts co-founder and former Amazo board member Bing Gordon said on Sozzi Unleashed. "And there was one year where we said, oh my God, it's $75 billion in capex. That would be like the top 10th country in the world … The board was freaked out early on when we weren't showing free cash flow. We were investing in the future. And it is kind of like the Anthropic story. Invest in the future. The market is usually pretty bad at figuring out the three- or four-year-out returns. And so this is the bet that the capex is going to pay off in that three- or four-year period, as it did with AWS."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the 'Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

item.title: US Offers Constellation $5 Billion Financing to Spur Nuclear
item.author: Ari Natter; Will Wade
item.description:
US Offers Constellation $5 Billion Financing to Spur Nuclear
2026-10-28
Por Ari Natter; Will Wade
https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/us-offers-constellation-5-billion-154220306.html
(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration is offering as much as $5 billion in financing to Constellation Energy Corp. to upgrade and modernize the nuclear operator's fleet of reactors in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The projects backed by the conditional loan commitment are expected to add nearly 1.1 gigawatts of electricity and help strengthen the grid and lower costs, according to the Energy Department. Constellation shares surged on the news.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright plans to announce the funding later Tuesday at an Illinois nuclear plant that will supply power to Alphabet Inc.'s Google.
"The Energy Department is accelerating President Trump's American nuclear renaissance and unlocking the full potential of our nation's nuclear fleet," Wright said in a statement. He said upgrades that increase output from existing nuclear facilities can expand electricity supply while supporting grid reliability and affordability for consumers and businesses.
Technology companies are driving interest in nuclear projects to power artificial intelligence. But new reactors can take a decade or more to permit and build. Upgrading components such as turbines can increase the output from existing plants, and is seen as a faster and cheaper way to deliver carbon-free fission electricity.
Constellation shares gained as much as 5.3%, and were up 2.8% to $259.63 at 11:39 a.m. in New York.
The Energy Department financing is part of President Donald Trump's push to expand nuclear power to meet growing electricity demand from data centers and support domestic manufacturing. The funding follows an executive order that set a goal of adding 5 gigawatts of capacity through upgrades at existing nuclear plants, 96% of which has been achieved, the department said.
Constellation is planning investments at six Illinois plants — Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities — as well as Calvert Cliffs in Maryland and Limerick in Pennsylvania to increase output from existing nuclear plants, the Energy Department said. The financing, through the department's Office of Energy Dominance Financing, also includes an option to fund future uprates at other Constellation facilities.
item.content:encoded:
US Offers Constellation $5 Billion Financing to Spur Nuclear

2026-10-28

Por Ari Natter; Will Wade

https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/us-offers-constellation-5-billion-154220306.html

(Bloomberg) -- The Trump administration is offering as much as $5 billion in financing to Constellation Energy Corp. to upgrade and modernize the nuclear operator's fleet of reactors in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania.

Most Read from Bloomberg

The projects backed by the conditional loan commitment are expected to add nearly 1.1 gigawatts of electricity and help strengthen the grid and lower costs, according to the Energy Department. Constellation shares surged on the news.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright plans to announce the funding later Tuesday at an Illinois nuclear plant that will supply power to Alphabet Inc.'s Google.

"The Energy Department is accelerating President Trump's American nuclear renaissance and unlocking the full potential of our nation's nuclear fleet," Wright said in a statement. He said upgrades that increase output from existing nuclear facilities can expand electricity supply while supporting grid reliability and affordability for consumers and businesses.

Technology companies are driving interest in nuclear projects to power artificial intelligence. But new reactors can take a decade or more to permit and build. Upgrading components such as turbines can increase the output from existing plants, and is seen as a faster and cheaper way to deliver carbon-free fission electricity.

Constellation shares gained as much as 5.3%, and were up 2.8% to $259.63 at 11:39 a.m. in New York.

The Energy Department financing is part of President Donald Trump's push to expand nuclear power to meet growing electricity demand from data centers and support domestic manufacturing. The funding follows an executive order that set a goal of adding 5 gigawatts of capacity through upgrades at existing nuclear plants, 96% of which has been achieved, the department said.

Constellation is planning investments at six Illinois plants — Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities — as well as Calvert Cliffs in Maryland and Limerick in Pennsylvania to increase output from existing nuclear plants, the Energy Department said. The financing, through the department's Office of Energy Dominance Financing, also includes an option to fund future uprates at other Constellation facilities.

item.title: Home prices continued to climb in August before mortgage rates surged
item.author: Claire Boston
item.description:
Home prices continued to climb in August before mortgage rates surged
2026-10-28
Por Claire Boston
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/home-prices-continued-to-climb-in-august-before-mortgage-rates-surged-145452131.html
Home price appreciation accelerated again in August while remaining below inflation.
The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller 20-City Composite Home Price Index, which measures home prices in 20 of the nation's largest metropolitan areas, rose 2.65% in August, from 2.47% in July.
The national index, which measures prices in a broader group of cities, rose 2.09%. The latest figures cover transactions that took place in June, July, and August, before mortgage rates crossed 7% and chilled sales.
Read more: How to get the lowest mortgage rates right now
The gains once again fell short of inflation, which hit 3.4% in August due to higher gas prices. Home prices have been falling in inflation-adjusted terms for the past 15 months, though they remain out of reach for many prospective buyers. The median home cost $429,100 in August, according to National Association of Realtors data, a record high for that month.
"Affordability … remains challenging," Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, said in a statement. "With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices."
Home price appreciation — or lack thereof — continues to vary widely across individual cities. Home prices in Chicago rose 6.7% in August, the fastest of any major US metro area. New York home prices rose 6.2%, while Cleveland's were up 4.3%. But home prices in Seattle fell 2%.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.
